article.title: Russell Vought Federal Grant Plan
article.author: Marcus Baram
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Kandy Fatheree runs the Summit County Sheriff’s Office in Ohio’s fourth-largest county. Randall Longenecker spent 30 years as a rural family doctor — delivering babies in small-town practice, then training a generation of physicians to do the same. The National Small Business Association has been a nonpartisan voice in Washington for nearly nine decades. None of them are the usual suspects in a fight with the administration of President Donald Trump. Yet all three filed formal objections to a proposed rule by the White House’s Office of Management and Budget that would hand political appointees sweeping authority over hundreds of billions of dollars a year in federal grants. In doing so, they joined opponents who range from county commissioners in Idaho to domestic violence advocates in New York City to a self-described free-market conservative at George Mason University, as well as community groups, nonprofits and foundations across the country. “Although I am sympathetic to the stated intention of this rule, I predict the consequences will be just the opposite of those intended,” Longenecker said in a comment to OMB in July, adding: “The unhealthy changes are so pervasive, I don’t know where to start.” The proposal would rewrite the rulebook governing how federal grants and cooperative agreements — such as funds for scientific research; broadband internet infrastructure; and state, local and tribal assistance — are awarded, managed and terminated. Senior political appointees would review them for alignment with administration priorities and executive orders, with final say over peer reviewers. Currently, such decisions go through a merit-based peer review process involving independent panels of nonpartisan scientists, clinicians, engineers and subject matter experts. But under the proposed overhaul, appointees could terminate any award, including active multiyear grants, if it no longer served “program goals, Federal agency priorities or the national interest.” That change worries Alex Tabarrok, a professor of economics at George Mason University, who was blunt in his critique of the proposal in a blog post last spring : “Political review of every award, peer review demoted, agency review promoted, termination whenever ‘priorities’ change. Chilling.” He called it “a nightmare of petty low-trust review of the kind that is already drowning science.” Related: Starbucks Gets a Tax Break: Families Pick Up the Tab The Office of Management and Budget — which plays a central role in implementing the president’s policy vision, management priorities and spending plans — said that the rule will bar grants from being used to “fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate” diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility and for “government sponsorship of gender ideology and other radical doctrines” and what the administration calls “child sexual mutilation,” its term for gender-affirming care. The proposal also prohibits using federal grant funding for voter registration, issue advocacy or political activity. The proposed rule, which was scheduled to take effect Oct. 1, drew close to 500,000 public comments, with reportedly 95% of them in opposition to the overhaul . Congress postponed its implementation to Dec.11 through the stopgap spending bill Trump signed in September. And the new Democratic-controlled Congress that takes office in January could stop or block the proposal through the appropriations process by explicitly barring the use of federal funds to develop, finalize, implement or enforce the rule. The White House and OMB did not respond to Capital & Main’s requests for comment. Supporters said the rule would impose needed discipline. Among them is the Heritage Foundation, whose Project 2025 document was written by current OMB head Russell Vought and which advocated for expanding executive power and reducing the independence of career civil servants and peer review processes. The conservative think tank has voiced support for the proposal’s DEI and gender-related restrictions and praised the proposal for establishing a single “control tower” to execute the administration’s agenda. Fiscal watchdog groups focused on immigration-related mandates and tighter payment controls against waste and fraud. The coalition opposing the proposal spans major universities, scientific and medical research institutions, civil liberties groups, local governments, nonprofits, law enforcement agencies and both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. Critics argued that the rule would fundamentally damage American innovation and public welfare by replacing the objective system of scientific peer review with political litmus tests administered by executive branch appointees. Opponents also said that the proposal unlawfully usurps Congress’s constitutional power to authorize federal spending. Serving and Protecting Fatheree’s Summit County Sheriff’s Office relies on federal grants for jail operations, mental health and substance abuse treatment, gun violence reduction, and narcotics and human trafficking cases, she said in a comment to OMB in July. Fluctuating requirements would burden agencies that “already face staffing shortages and limited administrative capacity,” she said, and letting agencies terminate funding “based on political considerations and policy priorities unrelated to the recipient’s actual performance undermines responsible long-term planning and introduces instability into otherwise reliable grant programs that have historically and consistently demonstrated positive public safety outcomes.” The Vera Institute of Justice, a nonprofit that focuses on immigration and criminal justice reform, flagged what it called a deeper vulnerability. The Community Oriented Policing Services, or COPS, program, which funds local police hiring, now exists only through annual appropriations rather than an underlying statute. “Ironically, considering the administration’s frequent statements of support for police and the DOJ’s $300 million Model Cities Initiative to ‘supercharge’ law enforcement, the new rule would place COPS funding—and the local law enforcement agencies that depend on it—in the same precarious position as discretionary grants for legal aid or violence intervention,” said Sam Feineh, Vera’s senior advocacy strategist , in a comment submitted to the OMB. Related: Trump's Coal Revival Is Raising Electric Bills—and Voters Are Fighting Back Cooperation Becomes Coercion Longenecker, a retired assistant dean emeritus of Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine who now lives in Bridgewater, Virginia, began applying for and implementing federal rural medical education grants through the federal Health Resources and Services Administration in 2010. The most recent grant he oversaw, to fund a technical assistance center for rural residency programs, has been successful, he said in an interview, but has become “increasingly difficult to work with because of so many layers of approval. Cooperation has become a coercion.” Colleagues still in grant leadership are “fearful of having a target on their back for anything they say.” “I experienced the same kind of micromanagement under multiple administrations,” Longenecker said. “The proposed way of managing grants would make it 10 times worse.” Rural programs, he added, are “the last mile” of a system of rules written by people “that have no clue how it actually works on the ground.” Michelle Salvaggio, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Oklahoma College of Medicine, said that local health departments depend on pass-through funding for disease surveillance, outbreak investigations and immunization programs. “During an outbreak or other public health emergency, a lack of reliable funding and the threat of grant termination without warning could cost lives by delaying detection, response and treatment efforts,” she said in a comment to OMB. The National Small Business Association, with more than 65,000 members, told OMB in a July letter that small firms “depend on a measure of predictability in their relationship with the federal government that this rule, however well-intentioned, would put at risk.” For a business that has hired staff, signed a lease or committed to subcontractors on the strength of a multiyear award, the group said, “that is a significant and largely uninsurable risk.” The Midnight Email The rule’s reach would extend beyond research grants. A provision allowing agencies to change the terms and conditions of awards after work has begun could touch some of the $900 billion a year in grants that flow to state and local governments, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities . In New Jersey, roughly 30% of the state budget comes from Washington, and much of what towns receive as state money started out as federal money, Melinda Rostal, an epidemiologist with the national volunteer group Defend Public Health , told Capital & Main. “They said we can’t run the town without federal funding,” she said of her own town council in Weehawken, New Jersey. Safe Horizon, a nonprofit that supports crime survivors across New York City, draws about 25% of its funding from federal dollars, Liz Roberts, CEO of Safe Horizon, told Capital & Main. It has already walked away from one grant — a federal Office on Violence Against Women award that required a certification committing the group to treat domestic violence “only as a crime” and to recognize “that there are only two sexes.” Those requirements were later struck down by a federal court . Related: GOP Candidate Exploits Data Center Backlash to Hit Solar, Wind in Wisconsin Declining the grant in 2025 cost the organization about $1 million a year and pulled advocates providing legal assistance from the Bronx Criminal Court, where the group has had a daily presence for decades, Roberts said. On Feb. 6, Roberts said, the group received an email at midnight which she explained stated that another grant for substance abuse and mental health services was “cut off effective immediately.” Forty-eight hours later, amid political pushback, the government reversed itself. “It would have taken services away from traumatized children,” Roberts said. The larger threat, she added, is pass-through money. New York City funds about 65% of the budget for its domestic violence shelters with federal money from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. If those funds were to be cut off under the proposed rule change, Roberts said, “it could literally result in us having to shut down our domestic violence shelters.” Safe Horizon runs and operates eight of them throughout the city, housing about 800 people a night. Political Litmus Test Elizabeth M. Ginexi, a former National Institutes of Health scientific program official, said that the rule would impose a “new political litmus test” on federal grants — an “impossible conflict” for organizations whose clients “are, by definition, the ones equity-focused programs are designed to reach.” As an example of funding that could be in jeopardy, she cited a drug crisis intervention grant in a rural Maine county of generational fishing families that reported a high number of LGBTQ youth. The Maine Center for Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, estimated the rule could put roughly $6 billion in federal funding to the state at risk. Rostal with Defend Public Health argued that the rule is an attempt to legalize what courts have blocked. Courts restored many early grant terminations at the start of the Trump administration in 2025 because agencies skipped required procedures, she said. “So now they’re going a step further and they’re changing the actual administrative procedures to make it legal,” she said. Related: Arizona’s Rising Electric Bills Are Reshaping the 2026 Midterms Rostal said that oversteps the executive branch’s authority. “It’s not the president’s job to decide whether or not we’re helping inner city kids or whether or not we’re maintaining rural hospitals,” she said. “That’s Congress’ decision.” Longenecker said he usually tries to offer agencies constructive tweaks. This time he came up empty. “I can’t even give a little piece of advice,” he said, “except to say this whole thing is so pervasively messed up that it just isn’t going to work.” Capital & Main
